summary: Tokyo rewards the specialist. Instead of one mall, dozens of focused worlds: twelve floors of stationery, a block of vintage denim, a basement dedicated to depachika sweets. Here's how to navigate by what you're after.

categories.title: Stationery
categories.body: Japan is the world capital of pens, paper, and planners. Try before you buy — every shop hands you paper samples.

picks.name: Itoya G.Ginza
picks.body: Twelve floors devoted to paper, pens, leather, and travel goods. 4F Smith pen counter is a pilgrimage site.

picks.name: Sekaido
picks.body: Art-supply mega-store. Cheapest prices on Copic markers, washi tape, sketchbooks in Tokyo.

picks.name: Bungu Box
picks.body: Tiny curator of high-end Japanese inks and fountain pens; house-made inks sell out.

categories.title: Japanese knives
categories.body: Sakai and Seki have forged blades for 600+ years. Kappabashi is Tokyo's kitchen-ware district; many shops engrave your name in kanji for free.

picks.name: Kama-asa Shoten
picks.body: Seven-generation knife house with English-speaking staff and a full catalogue of Japanese steels.

picks.name: Union Commerce
picks.body: Good mid-price range; great for a first Japanese chef knife under ¥15,000.

picks.name: Tsubaya Hocho-ten
picks.body: Handles vintage Yanagi-ba (sushi knives) as well as new stock; sharpening included.

categories.title: Vintage + thrift
categories.body: Shimokitazawa is the beating heart. Koenji is Shimokita's grungier cousin. Daikanyama Hillside and Omotesando for curated vintage at designer prices.

picks.name: Flamingo (Shimokitazawa)
picks.body: Chain for 70s-90s American vintage — Levi's, Carhartt, graphic tees — at fair prices.

picks.name: Chicago Harajuku
picks.body: Huge, cheap, well-organised by garment type. The kimono racks in the basement are the real find.

picks.name: Okura (Daikanyama)
picks.body: House of indigo aizome — modern Japanese workwear and scarves dyed in traditional vats.

categories.title: Anime, manga, retro games
categories.body: Akihabara for the whole spectrum; Nakano Broadway for rarer, dustier collector gold.

picks.name: Mandarake Complex
picks.body: Eight floors of used manga, vinyl figures, vintage toys. Know what you want — prices reward patient digging.

picks.name: Super Potato
picks.body: Retro game pilgrimage: Famicom, PC Engine, Saturn — fully tested, marked by condition.

picks.name: Nakano Broadway
picks.body: Four floors in a 1966 mall of 300+ small shops: manga, idol merch, vintage watches, niche everything.

categories.title: Electronics + audio
categories.body: Yodobashi Akiba for breadth. Audio-obsessed head to the basement bars and specialist rooms around Akihabara and Ochanomizu.

picks.name: Yodobashi Akiba
picks.body: Nine-floor mega-store with tax-free counter; decent prices, excellent variety.

picks.name: Dynamic Audio 5555
picks.body: Five floors of high-end audio — tube amps, €20,000 headphones, vinyl rooms. Listening welcomed.

picks.name: Disk Union (Shinjuku flagship)
picks.body: Eight floors of used CDs, vinyl, cassettes by genre. Jazz / J-pop / soul each get their own floor.

categories.title: Depachika (department-store food halls)
categories.body: Basement floors of every major department store — a ¥300 sample tour of top-tier wagashi, bento, pickles, sushi. 30 minutes before closing is the price-drop window.

picks.name: Isetan Shinjuku
picks.body: Tokyo's best depachika — basement 1 is pure theatre. Try the Ginza Sembikiya fruit sandos.

picks.name: Mitsukoshi Ginza
picks.body: Classic old-school depachika, strong on bento and wagashi.

picks.name: Takashimaya Nihombashi
picks.body: Sprawling, regional-product focused. Good for omiyage (take-home gifts).

categories.title: Luxury + high fashion
categories.body: Omotesando for architectural flagships; Ginza for heritage jewellers; Aoyama for Japanese avant-garde.

picks.name: Omotesando Hills + flagships
picks.body: Prada (Herzog & de Meuron), Dior (SANAA), Louis Vuitton (Jun Aoki), Tod's (Toyo Ito). Walk the avenue even if you buy nothing.

picks.name: Comme des Garçons Aoyama
picks.body: Rei Kawakubo's flagship plus Trading Museum — the conceptual side of Japanese fashion.

picks.name: Ginza Six
picks.body: Rooftop garden with a Tokyo skyline; six floors of international + Japanese brands; 1F teamLab installation.

categories.title: Traditional craft + workshops
categories.body: Not just buying — making. One-day classes in indigo dyeing, kintsugi, washi paper-making, wagashi decoration are well-run in English.

picks.name: Aizenkobo
picks.body: Indigo dyeing studio (150 years). Half-day dye-your-own-scarf class, advance booking.

picks.name: Kintsugi Library
picks.body: English-language workshops teaching gold-leaf pottery repair. Take your piece home after two sessions.

picks.name: Ozu Washi
picks.body: 350-year-old washi paper merchant with a small museum and paper-making classes.

categories.title: Shopping malls + complexes
categories.body: Vertical shopping cities — six to eight floors of fashion, food halls, cinemas, and observation decks. Often the easiest one-stop for travellers short on time.

picks.name: Shibuya Scramble Square
picks.body: 12 floors above Shibuya Station with Tsutaya Books, lifestyle brands, and Shibuya Sky observatory at the top.

picks.name: Tokyo Midtown
picks.body: Lower-key luxury complex anchored by The Ritz-Carlton, with Suntory Museum of Art and a quiet park.

picks.name: Roppongi Hills
picks.body: Six interconnected blocks; Mori Art Museum, Tokyo City View, plus 200+ shops. Best for design-forward labels and contemporary art.

picks.name: NEWoMan Shinjuku
picks.body: Curated department store atop the Shinjuku Bus Terminal — strong mix of independent Japanese designers and excellent depachika.

picks.name: Tokyu Plaza Omotesando
picks.body: The kaleidoscope-mirror entrance is a landmark; inside is Tommy Hilfiger, American Eagle, plus a rooftop garden facing Omotesando.

picks.name: Shibuya Hikarie
picks.body: Above-station tower with ShinQs depachika, theatre, and Sky Lobby views — calmer than Scramble Square next door.

categories.title: Boutiques + concept stores
categories.body: Where Tokyo sets the global agenda. Single-floor select shops for menswear, lifestyle goods, and Japanese designers you won't find at home.

picks.name: Beams Japan
picks.body: Six floors of Japan-only collaborations: tenugui, denim, ceramics, food. The flagship to bring home gifts you won't see again.

picks.name: United Arrows Harajuku
picks.body: House label plus carefully curated international brands; the Aoyama menswear store is the more refined sibling.

picks.name: Daikanyama T-Site
picks.body: Tsutaya bookstore + lifestyle complex set in a low-rise compound; arguably the most beautiful bookshop in Asia. Stay for breakfast at Ivy Place.

picks.name: A Bathing Ape (Bape Store Harajuku)
picks.body: Streetwear pilgrimage. Limited drops sell out fast — go on release Saturdays only if you're committed.

picks.name: Loopwheeler
picks.body: Slow-loomed sweatshirts on 1920s German machines — about 40 garments per machine per day. The standard premium hoodie.

picks.name: Dover Street Market Ginza
picks.body: Rei Kawakubo's seven-floor temple of luxury streetwear; everything from Comme des Garçons to Supreme drops in one elevator.

tax_free_note: Most shops displaying the "Japan. Tax-free Shop" logo refund 8-10% consumption tax if you spend ≥¥5,500 and show your passport at checkout. From 2026 the system is moving to a refund-on-departure model — keep receipts intact, don't open sealed bags until you've left Japan.
